title: The Corporate Board of Directors
description: The board of directors is the company’s highest governance body: elected by shareholders, it hires and fires the CEO, approves strategy and major transactions, oversees risk and financial integrity, and represents the owners’ interests. The structure: independent directors (no material ties to the company — the governance best practice is a majority independent), the chair (who runs the board; separate from the CEO in best practice — the combined chair-CEO concentrates power), and committees — audit (financial integrity, the most regulated), compensation (CEO and executive pay), nominating/governance (board composition), and risk. The disciplines: real independence (directors willing to challenge the CEO), information quality (boards govern on what management tells them — the information diet decides the governance quality), regular executive sessions (without management present), and annual self-evaluation. The failures are famous: captive boards that rubber-stamp (Enron’s board), CEO-dominated nominations, and audit committees that missed the fraud. Best practice keeps evolving — board diversity, climate competence, cybersecurity literacy — because the board’s job grows with the company’s complexity.
key_points: Hires/fires CEO; approves strategy; oversees risk
Majority independent; separate chair and CEO
Committees: audit, compensation, nominating, risk
Information diet decides governance quality
how_it_works: Shareholders elect directors; board charters committees, hires the CEO, approves major moves, oversees risk and integrity.
best_fit: Corporations of any scale; required for public companies.

title: Shareholder Primacy vs Stakeholder Capitalism
description: The defining governance debate: should companies serve shareholders first (Milton Friedman’s 1970 doctrine — the social responsibility of business is to increase profits) or all stakeholders (employees, customers, communities, the environment)? The shareholder-primacy era (1980s–2010s) brought stock-based CEO pay, buybacks, and quarterly capitalism — and the critiques: short-termism, wage stagnation, externalized costs. The stakeholder turn: the Business Roundtable’s 2019 statement (181 CEOs committing to all stakeholders), B-Corp certification growth, and ESG investing — with the counter-critique that stakeholder rhetoric without governance change is marketing. The serious middle: enlightened shareholder value — serving stakeholders as the strategy for long-term shareholder returns — and governance innovations (benefit corporation statutes, stakeholder advisory boards, long-term incentive metrics). The practical question for any board: whose interests may management trade off, and who decides? The answer belongs in the charter, not the press release.
key_points: Friedman 1970 vs Business Roundtable 2019
Shareholder era: buybacks, quarterly capitalism, critiques
Enlightened value: stakeholders as long-term strategy
Answer belongs in the charter, not the press release
how_it_works: Board defines the purpose and beneficiary hierarchy in the charter, aligns incentives and reporting, governs accordingly.

title: Founder Control Structures
description: Founder control structures let founders keep control while raising public capital: dual-class shares (Google, Meta, Ford — founders’ shares carry 10 votes each), staggered boards, and founder-friendly bylaws. The case for: founders think in decades while markets think in quarters — control structures protect long-term bets (Google’s moonshots, Meta’s metaverse spending) from activist pressure. The case against: entrenchment — failed founders cannot be removed, related-party deals go unchallenged, and the governance discount is real (studies show controlled companies trade at discounts). The middle instruments: sunset provisions (control expires after 7–10 years or on founder exit — the emerging best practice), majority-of-minority votes for conflicts, and independent board leadership alongside control. The trend: index funds and proxy advisors increasingly oppose perpetual control; sunset dual-class is becoming the acceptable form. The founder’s question: is the control protecting vision or ego? The honest answer decides the structure.
key_points: Dual-class shares: founders’ votes outweigh capital
Case for: decades thinking vs quarters pressure
Case against: entrenchment and governance discount
Sunset provisions: the emerging best practice
core_principles: Control should protect vision, not ego
how_it_works: Charter dual-class with sunset, maintain independent board leadership, submit conflicts to minority votes.
best_fit: Founder-led companies going public with long horizons.

title: Private Equity Governance
description: Private equity governance replaces public-market discipline with concentrated ownership discipline: the PE firm buys the company (often with leverage), installs a board it controls, and governs intensely for 5–7 years toward an exit. The operating system: the 100-day plan (immediate value-creation moves), the value-creation plan (the 3–5-year thesis — growth, margin, M&A), monthly operating reviews with teeth (the board knows the numbers weekly), management equity (the CEO and team own meaningful stakes — alignment through ownership), and leverage as discipline (debt service forces cash focus). The power: speed and accountability — decisions that took public companies quarters happen in weeks. The critiques: leverage risk (debt-funded dividends), short-termism (the exit horizon), and the fee load. The portable lesson for non-PE companies: concentrated attention, owned management, and a real value-creation plan — the governance intensity works without the leverage. Best fit: underperforming or under-managed companies needing intense transformation.
key_points: Concentrated ownership; 5–7-year exit horizon
100-day plan; value-creation thesis; monthly reviews with teeth
Management equity aligns through ownership
Leverage as cash discipline
how_it_works: Acquire, install controlled board, run 100-day plan, execute value thesis with monthly reviews, exit.

title: Venture Capital Governance
description: Venture capital governance balances founder drive with investor protection across the startup’s life. The instruments: the term sheet’s control provisions — board seats (investors take 1–2 of 3–5), protective provisions (veto over selling the company, raising senior debt, changing the charter), and pro-rata rights; the staged financing itself (each round’s valuation and terms re-underwrite the company); and information rights (monthly financials and metrics). The board’s role evolves: seed stage (advice and network), growth stage (hiring executives, strategy), late stage (exit preparation, governance professionalization). The healthy pattern: investors as value-add directors — customer introductions, talent, follow-on signaling — with control provisions as emergency brakes, not steering wheels. The failure modes: investor overreach (vetoing necessary pivots), founder-investor misalignment on exit timing, and the “board as audience” (founders performing instead of problem-solving). The best VC governance feels like a partnership with teeth: support normally, intervention when truly needed.
key_points: Board seats, protective provisions, staged financing
Board role evolves: advice, executives, exit prep
Control provisions as emergency brakes, not steering
Best feels like partnership with teeth
core_principles: Protect the investment; empower the founder
how_it_works: Negotiate balanced terms, build the evolving board, report transparently, use controls sparingly, align on exit.

title: ESOP and Employee Ownership Governance
description: Employee Stock Ownership Plans (US ESOPs — 6,500+ companies, 14 million participants) and worker cooperatives govern through employee ownership: the trust or cooperative owns the shares, employees build equity with tenure. The governance design: the ESOP trustee (fiduciary for employees’ retirement benefit — votes the shares, with pass-through voting on major issues in many plans), the board (often mixed: management, independents, employee representatives), and the ownership culture (open-book management, employee participation — ownership without voice is just a retirement plan). The disciplines: annual valuations (independent appraiser — the share price employees trust), repurchase obligation management (the company must buy back departing employees’ shares — plan the cash), and the ownership education (employees must understand the business to think like owners). Performance evidence: ESOP firms show higher productivity, lower turnover, and better downturn resilience. The failure: the ESOP as a tax/finance transaction without the ownership culture — the shares exist, the behavior does not change.
key_points: Trust/co-op owns; employees build equity with tenure
Trustee fiduciary; often mixed boards
Annual independent valuations; repurchase planning
Ownership culture required — shares alone do not change behavior
how_it_works: Establish trust/plan, value yearly, govern with employee voice, educate owners, manage repurchase cash.
best_fit: Mature profitable companies with committed workforces.

title: B-Corp and Benefit Corporation Governance
description: Benefit corporations (legal status in 40+ US states plus equivalents abroad) and B-Corp certification (B Lab, 5,000+ companies) hardwire stakeholder governance into the company’s legal DNA. The legal change: directors must consider stakeholders (workers, community, environment) — not just shareholders — and are protected when they do (the constituency statutes answer Friedman’s objection legally). B-Corp certification adds the verified standard: the B Impact Assessment scores governance, workers, community, environment, and customers (80+ points to certify), with recertification every three years. The governance practices: stakeholder advisory boards, public benefit reports, mission-locked charters (some with “mission guardians” holding veto over mission changes). The business case: talent attraction, customer loyalty, and long-term resilience — with the honest caveat that certification costs time and the legal form is still being tested in courts. Best fit: mission-driven companies wanting their values to survive ownership changes.
key_points: Legal: directors must consider stakeholders
B Impact Assessment: 80+ points, recertified 3-yearly
Mission locks survive ownership changes
Talent and loyalty returns; real certification cost
how_it_works: Adopt benefit form, certify via assessment, govern with stakeholder boards, report publicly, recertify.

title: DAO Governance: Code as Charter
description: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations govern via smart contracts and token votes: the rules execute as code, proposals pass by token-holder vote, treasuries disburse automatically. The experiments (MakerDAO’s stablecoin governance, ENS, Uniswap’s treasury) test whether governance can run without legal entities or managers. The mechanisms: proposal systems (forum discussion to on-chain vote), delegation (vote power delegated to active participants — addressing voter apathy), timelocks (passed proposals execute after delay, allowing review), and multisig safeguards (human override for emergencies). The lessons so far: voter apathy is extreme (most tokens never vote — plutocracy by default), smart-contract rigidity breaks on the unforeseen (The DAO’s 2016 hack and fork), and “code is law” fails the human disputes code cannot adjudicate. The serious synthesis emerging: code for the routine, humans for the exceptional — progressive decentralization as trust builds. Best fit: digital-native collectives where participants are pseudonymous and global.
key_points: Rules as smart contracts; treasuries disburse automatically
Mechanisms: proposals, delegation, timelocks, multisigs
Lessons: apathy, rigidity, code-can’t-adjudicate
Synthesis: code for routine, humans for exceptional
how_it_works: Deploy contracts, propose in forums, vote on-chain, execute via timelock, safeguard with multisig.

title: Family Business Governance
description: Family businesses — 70–90% of global enterprises — need governance for three overlapping systems: family, ownership, and business. The instruments: the family constitution (values, employment policies for relatives, dividend philosophy, conflict resolution — the family’s charter), the shareholders’ agreement (transfer restrictions, buy-sell provisions, valuation method — preventing the cousin feud from destroying the company), the board (with independents — the outside voice the family cannot provide itself), and the family council (the forum where family issues stay out of the boardroom). The disciplines: merit-based employment (family members meet the bar or do not join — nepotism destroys non-family talent), succession planning (the decade-long process, not the emergency), and separating family distributions from business reinvestment. The statistics drive the urgency: 30% survive to the second generation, 12% to the third — governance is the survival technology. The best family firms professionalize management while keeping family values: the family governs, professionals operate.
key_points: Three systems: family, ownership, business — govern each
Family constitution plus shareholders’ agreement
Independent directors; family council separate from board
30% reach generation two: governance is survival
how_it_works: Write the constitution, sign the agreement, seat independents, convene the council, plan succession early.

title: Audit Committees and Financial Oversight
description: The audit committee is governance’s financial immune system — and its failures are spectacular (Enron, Wirecard). The mandate: oversee financial reporting integrity, the external auditor relationship, internal audit, and whistleblower channels. The composition rules (post-Sarbanes-Oxley for public companies): all independent directors, at least one financial expert, and the external auditor reports to the committee — not management. The disciplines: executive sessions with auditors without management present (the meeting where the real issues surface), critical-accounting-policy reviews (where judgment lives — revenue recognition, reserves, impairments), internal-audit resourcing (the function’s budget and reporting line decide its courage), and the whistleblower channel’s independence and usage metrics. The committee’s information diet is the design variable: management’s presentations versus direct auditor and internal-audit access. The red flags committees must chase: auditor turnover, aggressive accounting in gray areas, and whistleblower channel silence (no reports means no trust, not no problems).
key_points: Mandate: reporting integrity, auditor relationship, whistleblowers
All independent; financial expert required; auditor reports to committee
Executive sessions without management
Red flags: auditor turnover, aggressive gray-area accounting
core_principles: Channels must be trusted to be used
how_it_works: Charter the committee, seat independents, meet auditors alone, review critical policies, resource internal audit, monitor channels.
best_fit: Public companies (required); best practice for large private.

title: Compensation Committees and Executive Pay
description: The compensation committee governs the pay that governs behavior — CEO and executive compensation design. The toolkit: base salary (the minority of pay), annual bonus (tied to yearly metrics), long-term incentives (stock/options vesting over 3–5 years — the alignment instrument), and the pay-for-performance linkage the committee must defend. The disciplines: independent committee (no CEO in the room for their own pay), independent compensation consultants (not management’s), peer benchmarking with disclosed peers (the Lake Wobegon ratchet — everyone above median — is the known failure), performance metrics tied to strategy (not just stock price), clawback provisions (recovering pay on restatements or misconduct — now mandated for US public companies), and the say-on-pay vote (shareholders’ advisory voice). The design tensions: pay enough to attract talent versus the optics and inequality critiques; long-term alignment versus the CEO’s actual horizon. The committee’s test: could it defend every element in public? If not, redesign.
key_points: Toolkit: salary, bonus, long-term incentives
Independent committee and consultants; disclosed peers
Clawbacks; say-on-pay; strategy-linked metrics
Test: defensible in public
how_it_works: Benchmark independently, design for strategy alignment, include clawbacks, disclose fully, face say-on-pay.

title: Risk Committees and Enterprise Risk
description: The risk committee (or the full board’s risk oversight) governs the enterprise’s risk appetite — what risks the company will take, and what it will not. The framework: the risk register (identified risks with owners, likelihood, impact), the risk appetite statement (the board’s explicit risk boundaries — in writing, not vibe), the three lines of defense (operations own risks, risk/compliance functions oversee, internal audit assures), and emerging-risk scanning (the horizon process for the risks not yet in the register). The disciplines: the CRO’s independence and board access (risk officers who report through the business get captured), scenario and stress testing (what breaks us? asked regularly), and the risk culture (compensation and promotion must not reward risk-taking the appetite forbids). Financial services regulators mandate much of this; the practices transfer everywhere. The failure mode: the risk function as paperwork — beautiful registers, unmanaged risks. The test: when did the board last decline an opportunity on risk grounds? If never, the appetite is decorative.
key_points: Risk appetite statement: explicit written boundaries
Three lines of defense model
CRO independence and board access
Test: has the board ever declined on risk grounds?
core_principles: Name the risks you will take
how_it_works: Write the appetite, maintain the register, empower the CRO, stress-test scenarios, align incentives, review quarterly.
best_fit: Regulated industries; any company with material risk.

title: Whistleblower Systems That Work
description: Whistleblower channels fail most often — and the failures enable the frauds. The working design: multiple channels (hotline, web, in-person — different reporters trust different media), genuine anonymity options (third-party operated, no caller ID, anonymous web), anti-retaliation with teeth (independent investigation of retaliation claims, consequences for retaliators — the policy that never punished retaliation teaches silence), and visible outcomes (reporters told what happened within the confidentiality limits — the black hole teaches futility). The governance: the channel reports to the audit committee, not management — the fox cannot guard the reports about the fox. The metrics that matter: report volume (zero reports means zero trust, not zero problems), substantiation rate, time to resolution, and — the gold standard — employee survey trust in the channel. The cultural prerequisite: leaders who thank reporters (even for uncomfortable reports) and act visibly. Sarbanes-Oxley and Dodd-Frank added legal teeth in the US; the EU Whistleblower Directive extends them. The channel’s paradox: its success is measured in problems surfaced — celebrate the reports.
key_points: Multiple channels; genuine anonymity; anti-retaliation with teeth
Reports to audit committee, not management
Zero reports means zero trust, not zero problems
Celebrate surfaced problems
how_it_works: Stand up independent channels, guarantee anonymity, investigate retaliation, report outcomes, measure trust.

title: Compliance Programs That Actually Comply
description: Effective compliance programs — the DOJ’s evaluation guidance is the standard — share design features the checkbox programs lack. Risk assessment first: the program targets the company’s actual risks (mapped and ranked), not generic training. Tone at the top with conduct in the middle: leaders model and middle managers reinforce — the program lives or dies in middle management. Right-sized resources and authority: the compliance officer with board access, budget, and the power to stop transactions. Training that teaches judgment (scenario-based, role-specific) not click-through slides. Confidential reporting plus investigation discipline (every report investigated, documented, resolved). Incentives aligned: compliance in performance reviews and promotions; misconduct with real consequences regardless of rank — the executive exception destroys the program. M&A and third-party due diligence (the acquired company’s sins become yours). Testing and updating: the program audited and improved, not filed. The DOJ’s three questions — is it well designed, resourced, and does it work in practice — are the design spec.
key_points: Risk-based design; tone at top plus conduct in middle
Resourced compliance officer with board access
Scenario training; aligned incentives; real consequences
DOJ’s three questions as the design spec
how_it_works: Assess risks, resource the function, train for judgment, investigate everything, align incentives, test and update.
best_fit: Regulated industries; any company with material compliance risk.

title: Succession Planning at the Top
description: CEO succession is the board’s most consequential decision — and the most commonly neglected until the emergency. The working system: the succession plan as a standing board agenda item (reviewed yearly, not when the CEO resigns), the internal pipeline (2–3 ready-now and ready-soon candidates, developed deliberately — stretch assignments, board exposure, executive coaching), the emergency plan (the interim CEO named in writing — the plan that fits on one page), and the external benchmark (knowing the market’s candidates keeps internal assessments honest). The disciplines: the CEO’s genuine participation (the threatened CEO sabotages succession — the board must require it), development over years not months, and the board’s independent judgment on readiness (management’s assessment needs the board’s verification). The data: planned successions outperform emergency ones dramatically — companies with named successors show better transition performance. The conversation to have: the CEO’s eventual departure is certain; only its planning is optional.
key_points: Standing yearly agenda item, not emergency response
Internal pipeline: ready-now and ready-soon candidates
One-page emergency interim plan
CEO participation required by the board
how_it_works: Maintain pipeline, develop candidates, name the interim, benchmark externally, review yearly with the board.

title: Board Composition and Refreshment
description: Board composition decides what the board can see — homogeneous boards have homogeneous blind spots. The design: the skills matrix (strategy, finance, industry, technology, risk, ESG — mapped against company needs, gaps recruited deliberately), diversity (cognitive and demographic — the evidence links diverse boards to better decisions and the talent pool demands it), independence (majority independent; independent chair or lead director), and refreshment (term limits or retirement ages — the 15-year director is management’s friend, not the owners’). The practices: annual board evaluation (real ones, with external facilitation periodically — the self-congratulatory survey helps nobody), director onboarding (the new director’s first-year education program), and the graceful exit conversation (the chair’s duty when a director’s contribution fades). The trend: boards adding technology, cybersecurity, and climate competence as those risks grow. The test: does the board’s composition match the company’s risk map? If the biggest risks have no director who understands them, recompose.
key_points: Skills matrix mapped to company needs
Diversity as decision quality, not optics
Term limits prevent management capture
Real evaluations with external facilitation
how_it_works: Map skills to risks, recruit gaps deliberately, evaluate yearly, refresh on terms, onboard thoroughly.

title: Shareholder Activism and Engagement
description: Shareholder activism — investors agitating for change — is governance’s market discipline, and boards need a playbook. The activist toolkit: stake-building, public letters, proxy fights, board-seat demands, and the “vote no” campaign. The legitimate triggers: sustained underperformance, misaligned pay, failed strategy, governance entrenchment. The board’s preparedness: know your vulnerabilities (the activist’s deck writes itself from public filings), engage major shareholders continuously (the relationship built before the crisis decides the crisis), evaluate the activist’s ideas on merit (some activists are right — dismissiveness destroys credibility), and have the response team ready (legal, IR, proxy solicitor). The engagement spectrum runs from constructive (private dialogue, board refreshment) to hostile (proxy contest). The governance lesson: the best defense is performance plus engagement — well-governed, well-performing companies with shareholder relationships rarely face hostile campaigns. The board that meets its owners only during fights has already lost.
key_points: Activist toolkit: stakes, letters, proxy fights, seat demands
Preparedness: know vulnerabilities, engage continuously
Evaluate ideas on merit — some activists are right
Best defense: performance plus engagement
how_it_works: Map vulnerabilities, maintain shareholder relationships, assess campaigns objectively, respond professionally.

title: Proxy Advisors and Institutional Voting
description: Institutional Shareholder Services (ISS) and Glass Lewis advise trillions in assets on proxy votes — their recommendations move elections. The mechanics: the advisors publish voting guidelines yearly, analyze each company’s proxy, and recommend for/against directors, pay plans, and proposals; many institutions vote largely with the recommendations. The influence debates: critics call them unaccountable power (robo-voting, one-size guidelines, conflicts in ISS’s consulting arm); defenders cite the alternative — institutions voting blind. The company’s playbook: know the guidelines (design pay and governance to pass them), engage the advisors directly (the annual meeting where you explain your context), and communicate with institutional holders (the advisors recommend; the holders decide — and large holders increasingly decide independently). The trend: the biggest asset managers building in-house stewardship teams and voting more independently — the advisors’ influence concentrating on smaller holders. The governance reality: proxy season is the annual exam — prepare all year.
key_points: ISS/Glass Lewis recommendations move elections
Debates: unaccountable power vs informed voting
Playbook: know guidelines, engage advisors, court holders
Big managers voting more independently
core_principles: Prepare all year for proxy season
how_it_works: Design to guidelines, engage advisors yearly, communicate with holders, monitor votes, improve.

title: Dual Fiduciary: The Benefit Director
description: Benefit corporations add a governance innovation: the benefit director — a board member charged with overseeing the public-benefit purpose. The role’s duties: ensure the board considers stakeholder impacts in major decisions, oversee the benefit report (the public account of stakeholder performance), and flag mission drift — the slow commercial erosion of purpose. The design questions: independence (the benefit director needs distance from management to challenge), expertise (stakeholder domains — environment, labor, community), and authority (advisory voice versus veto — most statutes give voice, some charters add teeth). The practice is young and the case law thin, which is both the opportunity and the risk: early adopters are writing the precedents. The portable insight for conventional boards: assign stakeholder oversight explicitly — the ESG committee, the stakeholder director — because the responsibility nobody owns is the responsibility nobody meets. Purpose needs a guardian with a seat at the table.
key_points: Benefit director oversees the public-benefit purpose
Duties: stakeholder consideration, benefit report, drift-flagging
Design: independence, expertise, authority level
Portable insight: assign stakeholder oversight explicitly
core_principles: Voice at the table, not just in the report
how_it_works: Charter the role, seat an independent expert, integrate into board process, publish benefit reports.

title: Governance for Private Companies
description: Private companies need governance proportionate to their scale — not public-company apparatus, but not founder fiat either. The scaling ladder: startup (advisory board — experienced advisors without fiduciary power, compensating for founder blind spots); growth (formal board with investor directors — fiduciary governance begins); mature private (independent directors added — the outside challenge voice); pre-IPO (public-company governance built early — audit committee, independent majority). The disciplines transfer at every rung: real financial oversight (someone independent reviews the numbers), documented major decisions (the discipline that prevents founder-memory disputes), related-party scrutiny (founder deals with the company need independent eyes), and succession thinking (the key-person risk named and managed). The family/private failure modes: the board as friends-and-family rubber stamp, the financials nobody independent sees, the succession nobody plans. The rule: governance should be one step ahead of scale — installed before the crisis that requires it.
key_points: Ladder: advisory board to fiduciary board to independents
Disciplines transfer at every rung
Independent financial oversight from early stages
Governance one step ahead of scale
how_it_works: Add governance per rung, keep financial oversight independent, document decisions, plan succession.

title: Crisis Governance: The Board in Emergencies
description: Crises reveal governance quality — the board’s emergency posture should be designed before the emergency. The architecture: the crisis protocol (who convenes, who decides, communication cadence — written and rehearsed), the board’s role clarity (oversight and support, not management — the board that tries to run the crisis response becomes the second crisis), information flow (direct lines to the crisis team, unfiltered by normal reporting), and the stakeholder communication plan (employees, customers, regulators, media — who says what, when). The disciplines: convene fast (hours, not weeks), protect the response team’s bandwidth (the board handles owners and regulators; management handles the crisis), document decisions (the post-crisis review needs the record), and plan the recovery governance (the crisis changes the company — strategy, leadership, and controls get revisited). The post-crisis review is mandatory: what the governance did right, what failed, what changes. Companies survive crises on management’s competence and boards’ composure — design for both.
key_points: Crisis protocol written and rehearsed before need
Board oversees and supports; does not manage the response
Direct unfiltered information lines
Mandatory post-crisis governance review
how_it_works: Write the protocol, clarify roles, rehearse, convene fast in crisis, support the team, review after.
t: Crisis Governance: The Board in Emergencies

title: Governance Ratings and Benchmarks
description: Governance quality is increasingly measured — and boards should know their scores. The raters: ISS QualityScore, MSCI governance ratings, and Glass Lewis assessments score board structure, pay alignment, shareholder rights, and audit quality. The uses: investors screen and engage on scores; activists cite them; companies benchmark against peers. The limitations: the scores measure structures more than behaviors (the independent board that never challenges scores well), one-size methodologies miss context, and gaming is possible (governance theater for the rating). The board’s approach: know your ratings, fix the legitimate gaps they reveal, explain the deliberate deviations (the controlled company explaining its sunset dual-class), and never govern for the rating — govern for the owners, and let the rating follow. The deeper benchmark is peer practice: the governance committee’s yearly review of what leading boards do differently. Ratings are the map; the territory is the boardroom’s actual behavior.
key_points: ISS, MSCI, Glass Lewis score governance structures
Uses: screening, engagement, activism, benchmarking
Limits: structures over behaviors; gameable
Govern for owners; let ratings follow
how_it_works: Track ratings, benchmark peers yearly, fix real gaps, explain deliberate deviations, focus on behavior.

title: The Future of Corporate Governance
description: Corporate governance is evolving under pressure from five forces. Technology: AI in boardrooms (decision support, risk monitoring), digital shareholder meetings, blockchain-based voting pilots. Stakeholders: the purpose debate maturing from rhetoric to charter changes and stakeholder metrics. Ownership: index-fund giants as permanent universal owners — voting for the market’s long term, engaging systemically (climate, governance standards). Regulation: expanding disclosure (climate, human capital, cybersecurity) and board-responsibility rules. Alternatives: DAOs, steward-ownership (purpose trusts holding companies — Patagonia’s 2022 transfer), and platform cooperatives testing post-shareholder forms. The through-line: accountability is widening (more stakeholders, more disclosure) while ownership concentrates (fewer, larger holders) — the paradox boards must navigate. The durable principles beneath the churn: independence enables truth, transparency enables trust, and the governed must be able to remove the governors. Forms change; those do not.
key_points: Five forces: tech, stakeholders, ownership, regulation, alternatives
Accountability widening while ownership concentrates
Steward-ownership and DAOs testing new forms
Durable: independence, transparency, removability
how_it_works: Monitor the forces, adapt charters and practices, experiment with new forms where fit, hold the principles.
best_fit: Boards planning for the next decade.

title: Designing Your Governance System
description: Designing governance is architecture: the blueprint before the building. The design sequence: define the company’s purpose and beneficiaries (the charter’s first question), choose the ownership and control structure (who owns, who controls, with what sunsets), design the board (composition, committees, independence, refreshment), allocate decision rights (the RACI/RAPID matrix for recurring big calls), build the oversight functions (audit, risk, compliance — resourced and independent), install the rhythms (board calendar, reporting, evaluations), and write the emergency posture. The design principles: fit over fashion (the startup does not need the public-company apparatus), independence grows with scale and stakes, transparency by default (secrets need reasons), and review triggers (revisit on scale doubling, ownership change, or crisis). The governance document — the charter, bylaws, and committee charters as one coherent set — is the system’s source code. Review it yearly; refactor when it no longer describes reality.
key_points: Sequence: purpose, ownership, board, rights, oversight, rhythms, emergencies
Fit over fashion; independence with scale
Transparency by default
The charter set is the system’s source code
how_it_works: Work the sequence deliberately, write the coherent document set, install rhythms, review yearly.
